readings: For each account, work out its share of all orders: its order count divided by the total number of orders (`order`). For the accounts whose share is above the average share, give one row with the total number of orders they have, their average share, and on average how far above the average share they are. Do not round. Consider only accounts that have at least one order, so the average share is taken over accounts appearing in `order`.

For each account, work out its share of all orders: its order count divided by the total number of orders (`order`). For the accounts whose share is above the average share, give one row with the total number of orders they have, their average share, and on average how far above the average share they are. Do not round. Consider every account in the account table, counting accounts with no orders as share 0 when computing the average share.
queries:
WITH acc AS (
    SELECT account_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt,
           CAST(COUNT(*) AS REAL) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM `order`) AS share
    FROM `order`
    GROUP BY account_id
),
avg_share AS (
    SELECT AVG(share) AS a FROM acc
)
SELECT SUM(acc.cnt) AS total_orders,
       AVG(acc.share) AS average_share,
       AVG(acc.share - avg_share.a) AS average_excess
FROM acc, avg_share
WHERE acc.share > avg_share.a;
WITH c AS (
    SELECT a.account_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS cnt
    FROM account a
    LEFT JOIN `order` o ON o.account_id = a.account_id
    GROUP BY a.account_id
),
s AS (
    SELECT account_id, cnt, cnt * 1.0 / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM `order`) AS share
    FROM c
),
av AS (
    SELECT AVG(share) AS avg_share FROM s
)
SELECT SUM(s.cnt) AS total_orders,
       AVG(s.share) AS avg_share,
       AVG(s.share - av.avg_share) AS avg_above_average
FROM s, av
WHERE s.share > av.avg_share;
